title: Dying in the Word
hook: he speaks of dying to ego through the Word and living truly

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmukh and manmukh: two directions of the face, not two kinds of people. Your line was face the good. When did you catch yourself turning? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

Some phrases sound alarming until you see them up close. Take an argument at the dinner table. Someone is sure they're right, the clever reply is loading, and then, for no reason anyone can see, you let it go. The reply dies unspoken. Something small in you has to lose for the evening to be saved. Guru Amar Das has a phrase for a much larger version of that moment, and it's a bold one: to die in the Word. It sounds like an ending. In his hymns it's the start of living.
screen: `THE CLEVER REPLY, LOADING.` → `SOMETHING SMALL HAS TO LOSE.` → `TO DIE IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: In Sri Rag, he says it like this, paraphrased: whoever dies in the Word stays dead, and does not die a second time. Through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold. So what dies? Not the body. Haumai, the ego, the I, I, mine we met at the start of his voice. The Word, sabad, is the Guru's teaching; dying in it means letting that teaching do what ego never allows, which is to put something other than me at the center. And notice the strange promise: you don't die a second time. Some readers take it this way: once ego's grip is broken in the Word, the fear of death and the round of coming and going lose their hold. Ten days ago, Guru Angad's salok gave this a picture: dying while alive. Sikhs call it jivat marna. It doesn't mean giving up on life. It means living fully with the self out of the driver's seat. Here's why this matters on an ordinary day. Ego doesn't usually die in one heroic moment. It dies in dinner-table moments: the reply you don't fire, the credit you don't grab, the grudge you put down. Each of those is a small rehearsal of the big thing. And the line is clear about the direction this leads. Not into gloom. What follows the dying, in the verse, is finding the Lord, and a love for the Name that takes hold. That's the paradox the Guru hands us today.
screen: `DIES IN THE WORD, DIES NO MORE.` · `WHAT DIES: THE EGO'S GRIP.` · `JIVAT MARNA: DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `SMALL DEATHS AT THE DINNER TABLE.` · then, large: `DIE TO EGO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one ego-want die. Settle, and let the breath slow. Find one small want that's mostly about you being seen, being right, or being first. Wanting the last word in a text thread. Wanting someone to notice what you did. Hold it gently, and look at it. Then, on a long breath out, set it down. You may need to set it down more than once. That's normal. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the word that fills the space it leaves. The bell holds the time.
Dying in the Word. Letting ego's grip break through the Guru's teaching, so that, as Guru Amar Das says, you need not die a second time, and can begin to live truly. Today's word.
Your line: die to ego. Today, let one clever reply, one bid for credit, or one grudge die quietly, and see what lives in its place. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet the idea of dying in the Word in Guru Amar Das's hymns, sung in kirtan and explained in katha; it is lived through daily remembrance of the Name and seva done without seeking credit.

fork.reveal: it's haumai that dies, and the result isn't an ending: through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold.
